summary: Defines an SMTP extension, ETRN, that lets a client ask a server to start processing its queue of mail waiting for a given host. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If your mail is waiting in the post office because you were away, this lets you knock on the door and say please send what you have for me now.

questions: how to trigger remote mail queue processing
how does etrn differ from turn
what are the etrn reply codes
subtitle: ETRN lets a mail client ask a server to start sending the mail it is holding for that client.

tldr.problem: Sites with only transient connections need a way to make their provider send queued mail right away, and the older TURN command can be abused because the remote host name is not verified.
tldr.mechanism: The ETRN extension adds one command that names the host or domain to process. The server then opens a new SMTP connection towards that host instead of reversing the current one.
tldr.outcome: A client can trigger delivery of waiting mail without the TURN security loophole, and the server stays free to refuse the request.

today: RFC 1985 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the ETRN extension to SMTP.

sections.title: Why ETRN Exists
sections.content:
Many small companies keep only transient connections to their service providers to save money. Some also depend on mail arriving quickly, so forcing the provider's queues to run is better than waiting for the retry timeout.

The TURN command of RFC 821 could do this, but it reverses the direction of the SMTP connection and trusts the remote host to be honest about its name. The RFC says there is no documented stipulation for checking the host name given in HELO or EHLO, so a rogue system could use TURN to download the mail for a site other than itself. Because of this, most SMTP and ESMTP implementations do not implement TURN.
sections.eli5: The old way handed your mail to whoever said they were you. That was risky, so a safer way was needed.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
The extension uses the mechanism of RFC 1425. It is named "Remote Queue Processing Declaration". The server advertises the EHLO keyword ETRN, with no parameters. One new verb, ETRN, takes a single parameter naming the client or clients to process for. No other verbs are added.

The security fix is in how it works: the server is asked to start a new connection aimed at the specified client, rather than trusting the current connection. The server therefore has much more certainty that it is talking to the right SMTP client. The RFC describes it as a more immediate version of the retry queues in most SMTP implementations. Since the command names the host, the server can also decline for local administrative reasons.
sections.eli5: Instead of handing mail to the person at the door, the post office phones the address it has on file and sends the mail there.

sections.title: The ETRN Command and Its Replies
sections.content:
The syntax is ETRN [<option character>]<node name> followed by a CR LF. It may be issued at any time in a session when no transaction is in progress, so it is illegal between MAIL FROM: and the end of the DATA exchange. The node name must be a fully qualified domain name, which may refer to a CNAME or MX pointer in the DNS. If the node has several aliases, several ETRN commands may be needed.

On receipt, the server decides locally whether to honour the request. If it does, it should force its retry queues to start sending to that site over another SMTP connection. There is no requirement that a connection occur, or that it occur within any time frame. The command should return immediately, since queue processing can take an indeterminate time.

The reply codes are 250 (queuing started), 251 (no messages waiting), 252 (pending messages started), 253 (a count of pending messages started), 458 (unable to queue), 459 (node not allowed, with a reason), 500 (syntax error) and 501 (syntax error in parameters). A plain 250 does not promise that messages will be sent. The 251, 252 and 253 codes, if the server supports them, give the client more information, including a way to tell when no pending messages remain.
sections.eli5: You send one short request naming who the mail is for. The post office answers with a number telling you whether it will help, has nothing for you, or says no.

sections.title: Client Behaviour, Subdomains and Queues
sections.content:
If the client gets a 500-level error, it should assume the extension is unsupported or implemented incorrectly, and should not send more ETRN commands for aliases. A 250 means the server found the request satisfactory and will send queued mail, which may take a while through a very large retry queue. A 400-level reply means the server supports the command but does not want to accept it as given, usually because the client is not on a list of accepted nodes. The 459 code explains why.

Two option characters widen the request. With @ in front of the node name, any name ending in that suffix is released, so ETRN @foo.com may release mail for fred.foo.com, a.b.c.d.e.f.g.foo.com or foo.com. With the hash sign, the node name is treated as a queue name instead, as in ETRN #uucp to flush a UUCP queue. Queue names are a local matter and a client cannot list them.

A minimal client may simply use its own host name. A minimal server may start processing all queues for any request and always return 250, so 458 would never be seen.
sections.eli5: Adding an at-sign means please send everything for my whole neighbourhood. Adding a hash means please empty this particular mailbag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that ETRN does not compromise the security of existing SMTP or ESMTP, because it only shortens the time a client waits before its messages are retried.

Servers should still take precautions with the at-sign and hash-sign options and allow them only for systems where they make sense. Without sanity checking of the parameters, congestion could result. The RFC's example is a request to release @com, which would release mail for any address ending in com.
sections.eli5: The post office should not let one person ask for the mail of a whole country at once, because that would cause a traffic jam.

sections.title: An Example Session
sections.content:
The RFC gives a sample session. The client sends EHLO and the server lists ETRN among its extensions. A bare ETRN gets 500 Syntax Error, and ETRN localname gets 501 Syntax Error in Parameters. A request for uu.net is refused with 458.

Successful runs show 250 for a started queue, or alternatively 251 for no waiting messages, 252 for pending messages and 253 with the count, such as 14 pending messages for mysoft.com. A name the server cannot resolve gets a 459 reply.
sections.eli5: The example shows some tries that go wrong and some that work, with the post office answering each one with a number.

data.title: ETRN session
data.code:
C: EHLO ymir.claremont.edu
S: 250-sigurd.innosoft.com
S: 250-EXPN
S: 250-HELP
S: 250 ETRN
C: ETRN
S: 500 Syntax Error
C: ETRN localname
S: 501 Syntax Error in Parameters
C: ETRN uu.net
S: 458 Unable to queue messages for node uu.net
C: ETRN sigurd.innosoft.com
S: 250 OK, queuing for node sigurd.innosoft.com started

items.label: Queuing started
items.desc: Queue processing started for the node.

items.label: No messages waiting
items.desc: No messages are waiting for the node.

items.label: Pending messages started
items.desc: Pending messages for the node started.

items.label: Counted messages started
items.desc: A stated number of pending messages started.

items.label: Unable to queue
items.desc: The server could not queue messages for the node.

items.label: Node not allowed
items.desc: The node is refused, with a reason.
